w: Outdoor escalators climb a hillside barrio once ranked the world's most dangerous urban area; every wall beside them carries murals of doves, raised fists and white cloths, painted by former residents who turned a scarring 2002 military raid into a story told through spray paint.
s: Escalators through a barrio's mural-covered rebirth
why: A once-notorious hillside slum reinvented itself as one of South America's most powerful open-air galleries of resilience.

w: Twenty murals wrap the facades of a hillside barrio in a labyrinth of stairways, painted in the 1990s by Chilean masters including Roberto Matta and Nemesio Antunez as a museum with no walls or tickets. Steps zigzag past Pablo Neruda's La Sebastiana house and bay views below.
s: An open-air museum built into a hillside barrio
why: One of the earliest and most influential open-air mural museums in Latin America, painted by the country's leading artists.

w: A cobbled alley off Rua Goncalo Afonso takes its name from a 1980s Batman graffito that started a free-for-all; art students layered on psychedelic and cubist designs until every surface, sidewalks included, vanished under paint. Pieces are repainted within weeks, never the same twice.
s: A bohemian alley repainted every few weeks
why: One of Brazil's longest-running open graffiti walls, credited with regenerating the whole Vila Madalena district.

w: Chilean-born artist Jorge Selaron began tiling the crumbling steps outside his house in 1990, using coloured fragments for the Brazilian flag before visitors from over sixty countries donated tiles of their own. The 215-step staircase, spanning Lapa and Santa Teresa, was never declared finished.
s: 215 mosaic-tiled steps donated by the world
why: A single artist's decades-long, ever-growing folk-art staircase that became one of Rio's most photographed landmarks.

w: Over 200 murals cover this bohemian clifftop barrio, blending social commentary with pure colour; muralist Jade Rivera keeps a studio here, and the Montero Bernales bridge carries the district's largest single mural space. A 2015 whitewashing crackdown backfired, sparking an annual repainting festival.
s: A bohemian clifftop barrio turned open gallery
why: Grew from scattered 2000s graffiti into Lima's densest and most curated concentration of street murals.

n: El Cuento de los Loros mural
w: Muralist Martin Ron spent sixteen days with two collaborators covering a 412-square-metre facade at Holmberg and Pedro Ignacio Rivera with parrots, a giant Michelangelo's David and a skateboarding, hyperreal portrait, painted in 2013 as the city's largest mural to date.
s: A four-storey hyperreal mural of parrots and David
why: Was the largest single mural in Buenos Aires when painted, a landmark of the city's hyperrealist muralism scene.

w: A former Zapotec village swallowed by Oaxaca centuries ago, its cobbled streets carry murals by local and Zapotec artists layered onto candy-coloured colonial facades. Calaveras and jaguar motifs recur throughout, blending folk symbolism with contemporary social themes.
s: Candy-coloured colonial streets full of murals
why: One of Mexico's most concentrated blends of colonial architecture and contemporary Zapotec-inflected muralism.

w: Lithuanian artist Ernest Zacharevic's 2012 mural 'Little Children on a Bicycle', a painted boy and girl astride a real bicycle bolted to the wall, launched George Town's rise as Malaysia's street-art capital during that year's festival. He returns often to restore the fading, heavily touched piece.
s: A painted boy and girl on a real bicycle
why: The single mural credited with putting Malaysian street art on the world map, named among the Guardian's best of 2013.

w: Fox Street, running through the redeveloped Jewel City blocks, carries some of the more than fifty murals commissioned when Maboneng's industrial shells were repurposed; painters were briefed to reflect Johannesburg's mixed cultures. Derelict warehousing a decade ago, now an open-air gallery.
s: Fifty-plus murals through a reborn industrial zone
why: Sub-Saharan Africa's densest cluster of commissioned murals, credited with regenerating a derelict inner-city precinct.

w: More than fifty large-scale works by Faith47, Falko One and other artists cover Salt River's warehouse walls, painted mainly during the annual International Public Art Festival that Baz-Art has run since 2017. The murals confront gentrification while celebrating local legends and history.
s: Festival murals confronting a gentrifying quarter
why: Cape Town's largest sanctioned mural trail, produced by an annual festival that brings in international street artists every year.

w: Community organisers Kibera Walls for Peace and Kibera Creative Arts began painting the corrugated-iron walls of Nairobi's largest informal settlement in the 2010s, turning them into a running dialogue on poverty and survival, led partly by Bankslave, dubbed Kenya's graffiti godfather by CNN.
s: Informal-settlement walls turned peace murals
why: A grassroots mural movement that reframed one of Africa's largest slums as a canvas for community dialogue rather than decay.

w: Since 2010 the NGO Yataal Art, Wolof for 'spreading art', has invited over a hundred Senegalese and international painters into one of Dakar's oldest quarters, asking each family's permission before a wall is touched. Frescoes on health, begging and environment cover hundreds of facades.
s: A hundred-plus artists painting a historic quarter
why: A rare street-art project built on door-to-door consent from residents rather than top-down commissioning.

w: The Urban Forms Foundation has covered more than 170 gable ends since 2009, commissioning Polish painters and international names such as Os Gemeos, Eduardo Kobra, Inti and Aryz on the city's blank post-industrial facades. Some pieces incorporate neon that only activates after dark.
s: 170-plus gable-end murals across a post-industrial city
why: Ranked second globally for urban art density behind New York by a 2014 survey, the largest permanent mural collection in Poland.

w: Houses crammed along the once flood-ravaged banks of the Code river carry rainbow-roofed murals and cartoon graffiti, part of a kampung revival begun by architect Romo Mangunwijaya decades ago. The colour transformed a settlement once written off as a slum into a photographed street-art strip.
s: A rainbow-roofed kampung along a once-flooded river
why: One of Southeast Asia's most striking examples of street art used for genuine riverside slum regeneration.

w: A cobbled laneway off Flinders Street has carried wall-to-wall paste-ups and spray work since the 1990s, hosting international names including Shepard Fairey and Invader alongside Melbourne regulars Ha-Ha, Prism and Rone. Matt Adnate's 23-metre 'Aboriginal Boy' remains its most photographed piece.
s: Melbourne's original wall-to-wall graffiti laneway
why: The laneway that established Melbourne's international reputation as a street-art city, still repainted almost daily.

w: A once-derelict office street was handed to international artists for the 2011 See No Evil festival, and within days its multi-storey gable ends carried some of the largest legal murals in Europe, including Nick Walker's stencil-and-satire pieces near Banksy's 'Well Hung Lover'.
s: Multi-storey murals from Bristol's See No Evil festival
why: One of Europe's largest concentrations of sanctioned high-rise murals, seeding Bristol's ongoing Upfest tradition.

w: A hillside village below Naksan Park, once slated for demolition and home mostly to poor and elderly residents, was repainted by around seventy artists under a 2006 revitalisation project. Crowds grew so heavy that in 2016 frustrated residents quietly painted over some murals themselves.
s: A demolition-slated hillside saved by seventy muralists
why: One of the first government-led mural regenerations in Asia, and a cautionary tale about overtourism in a living neighbourhood.

w: Narrow lanes around Ki Ling Lane and Shek Chan Lane were repainted under an urban-revitalisation scheme, filling steep staircases and shophouse walls with colour; the best-known piece, near MTR exit B3, shows a girl watering plants beside a rainbow-striped stairway repainted each HKwalls festival.
s: A rainbow staircase in a revitalised shophouse quarter
why: One of Hong Kong's densest mural concentrations, refreshed annually by the HKwalls street-art festival.

w: A narrow alley off one of Bangkok's oldest streets was the epicentre of the 2013 and 2016 Bukruk Urban Art Festivals; Alex Face's wide-eyed rabbit Mardi, Bonus TMC's bears and tigers, and Lolay's bone-white creatures still line the walls, best seen once street vendors clear in late afternoon.
s: Bukruk-festival murals down a colonial-era alley
why: Bangkok's original street-art alley, still largely intact more than a decade after its founding festival.

w: Bucharest's best-known mural strip is repainted every year during the Street Delivery festival, when the road closes to traffic and artists work outdoors before crowds. Pisica Patrata, one of Romania's most recognised street artists, has used its walls to flag the capital's neglected buildings.
s: A festival street repainted live every year
why: The anchor site of Bucharest's Street Delivery festival, Romania's longest-running open-air urban art event.

w: Warehouse facades along the Sava river carry some of Belgrade's most striking murals, including Remed's many-armed 'La Santa de Belgrade' and Blu's giant figure devouring a tree of corporate towers. Much of the quarter was later demolished for the Belgrade Waterfront redevelopment.
s: River-warehouse murals surviving a vanished quarter
why: Serbia's most concentrated mural district, its story bound up with the controversial redevelopment that erased much of it.

w: A self-declared bohemian 'republic' across the river from Vilnius's Old Town, complete with its own constitution and a trumpet-blowing angel statue, wears murals and installations down almost every side street off Uzupio Street, anchored by the studios of the Uzupis Art Incubator.
s: Murals through a self-declared artists' republic
why: A mock breakaway republic where street art, sculpture and constitution-writing artists share the same few blocks.

w: As mayor from 2001, artist Edi Rama had grey communist-era apartment blocks along the Lana river repainted in bright geometric colour, calling it his 'supreme form of conceptual art'. Locals reported paying more taxes and littering less once their buildings turned orange, purple and lime green.
s: Communist blocks repainted as conceptual art by a mayor
why: A rare case of a government using large-scale colour as literal civic policy, credited with lifting local morale and tax compliance.

w: Stavanger has hosted the Nuart festival since 2001, one of the oldest dedicated street-art events anywhere, drawing names like Dolk and Martin Whatson to leave permanent, legal works across the old town. Nearby Ovre Holmegate's rainbow-painted shopfronts complement the festival's murals.
s: A rainbow street feeding Norway's oldest art festival
why: Home to one of the world's longest-running street-art festivals, which built Norway's reputation as a serious urban-art destination.

n: MIAU Unfinished Museum of Urban Art
w: A shrinking mountain village near a landfill that locals resented turned protest into invitation: since around 2013 the MIAU festival has housed and fed visiting artists in exchange for murals on old stone houses, filling streets with painted robots, giant cats and cyborgs each summer.
s: A mountain village that painted away its stigma
why: A depopulating rural village that reversed its decline through an annual, resident-hosted mural festival with no gallery walls at all.

w: In June 2014 the Paris gallery Itinerrance brought 150 artists from 30 countries to the whitewashed village of Erriadh, using over 4,500 spray cans to paint 250 murals across its traditional Djerban architecture in just ten days. More than 300 works now cover what was once a quiet backwater.
s: 150 artists painted an entire whitewashed village
why: One of the largest single street-art interventions ever staged, transforming a traditional village into an open museum in ten days.

w: Graffiti has covered this bohemian square's walls since the late 1980s, tolerated here more openly than almost anywhere else in the city, where locals say artists paint 'pretty much anywhere'. A corner building on Rue Pastoret carries one of Thoma Vuille's grinning Monsieur Chat characters.
s: A bohemian square where graffiti goes almost anywhere
why: Marseille's longest-tolerated open graffiti zone, painted continuously since the late 1980s.

w: Known during the 2011 uprising as the Street of the Eyes of Freedom, the walls beside Tahrir Square filled with portraits of protesters killed by security forces. Authorities whitewashed the murals repeatedly through 2011 and 2012, and artists kept returning to repaint them each time.
s: Revolution murals repeatedly painted and erased
why: The clearest physical record of Egypt's 2011 revolution, fought over in paint between artists and the state for years afterward.
